  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Train Conductor
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Vignette:
Omar had always loved the rhythm of the rails, the steady, metronomic clatter that had been the soundtrack to his life for seven years as a train conductor. That rhythm was shattered four months ago on a bitterly cold Tuesday in February. It was the last run of his shift, the air sharp and frigid against the windows of his cab. The sudden, violent screech of the emergency brake was a sound he knew but had never initiated. When the train shuddered to a halt between stations, a frantic call came over the radio. He was the first one on the scene. The image was seared into his mind: a young man, a fall from the platform, the devastating aftermath spread across the tracks. What he remembers most vividly, more than the initial shock, was kneeling on the concrete of the service walkway, the intense, biting cold seeping through the fabric of his uniform trousers into his skin, a cold that felt like it was freezing him from the inside out. He remembers the unnatural red against the grey ballast and the impossible angles of the man’s limbs.

In the weeks that followed, the world began to feel like a series of tripwires. The cold was the first thing he noticed. A chilled countertop under his palm, the draft from an open window, or the specific damp cold of a refrigerated aisle in the grocery store would send a jolt through his body, and for a second, he would be back on that walkway, the smell of ozone and iron in the air. At work, his cab, once a place of comfort, became a cage where he was forced to watch for danger. He found himself scanning the platforms with an intensity that left his eyes burning and his neck stiff. Every person standing near the yellow line was a potential catastrophe. His colleagues would give him the "all clear," but their words were meaningless noise. He was certain they couldn't see what he could see—the subtle shift in someone's weight, the vacant look in their eyes. He had to be the one to watch, because he was the only one who truly understood how quickly everything could go wrong.

The vigilance followed him home. Sleep became an enemy. Omar would lie in bed for hours, his body rigid, listening to the hum of the refrigerator and the distant city traffic. He was convinced that if he allowed himself to drift off, he would miss a crucial sound, a warning that something terrible was about to happen. He felt he had to remain on guard, a lone sentinel responsible for an unseen perimeter. The exhaustion was bone-deep, a heavy cloak he couldn't take off. It made concentrating at work nearly impossible.

His world shrank. A few weeks ago, a passenger boarded his train with a heavily bandaged hand, a dark red seeping through the white gauze. Omar felt his heart hammer against his ribs, his breath catching in his throat. He had to retreat to his cab, gripping the controls until his knuckles were white, unable to look at the man for the rest of the journey. He knew it was just a minor injury, but his body screamed otherwise. The sight of blood, even a child’s scraped knee at the park, felt like a personal threat. He started making excuses to avoid friends, especially one who worked as a paramedic, terrified of what stories or sights he might bring with him. Last week, his supervisor took him aside after he held his train at a station for two minutes, refusing to depart until a teenager leaning against a pillar moved back, despite the platform guard's assurances. The formal warning for the delay felt less like a punishment and more like confirmation of what he already feared: he was losing control. It was the fear of losing his job, the one piece of his old life he was desperately clinging to, that finally propelled him to seek help. He doesn't know if he can ever feel safe again, but he is hoping to learn how to believe it when someone tells him he is.
